 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES,

       Intervenors Solana Ranch Company, Solana Development, LP, Don Al Ringer, and

CEDON Realty, Ltd. (collectively, the “Solana Intervenors” or “Solana”) (Party No. 217) submit

this Reply Brief and would respectfully show the following:

   I. INTRODUCTION

       1.      Solana Development, LP is the owner and developer of Solana Ranch, a large-scale

master-planned community located in Williamson and Bell Counties along the Interstate 35

corridor between Georgetown and Temple. The property encompasses approximately 8,000 acres,

most of which is dedicated to an active development effort planned to include approximately

14,000 residential units together with commercial, civic, recreational, and open space uses. Solana

Ranch Co. owns land adjacent to that owned by Solana Development, LP. The land owned by

Solana Ranch Co. will be preserved in its legacy agricultural and natural uses as described in the

testimony of Michael Michaux. The existing extensive wildlife habitat on the Solana Ranch Co.

property will be integrated with designated wildlife habitat on the Solana Development, LP

property. Among the other negative impacts of Route 894, the integrated wildlife habitat would

be adversely affected by the bisection of the properties. Don Al Ringler and CEDON Realty, Ltd.

own Ringler Ranch, a separate adjacent property in Bell County managed for wildlife,

conservation, and family use, that would be directly and adversely affected by the introduction of

HVTL infrastructure in the same area.

       2.      Route 894 bisects the developable core of the Solana Development property and

the reserved Solana Ranch. It also places major 765-kV transmission infrastructure immediately

adjacent to Ringler Ranch. The Solana Intervenors oppose Route 894 and any route utilizing Links

E52, F1, F20, F21, F32, or F33. Route 894 fails to satisfy the statutory routing criteria set forth in

PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D) and PUC Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B).

 II.     REPLY REGARDING NEED.

      A. Background.

        3.       After reviewing the Applicants Initial Brief and the Initial Briefs of the other

intervenors cited below, the Solana Intervenors respectfully submit that the Joint Applicants have

failed to meet their burden to show the need for this project. Applicants attempt to wrap all three

import paths together, as opposed to independently justifying each one, raises concerns that merit

consideration.

        4.       ERCOT conducted the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) study on Permian

Oil & Gas plus large loads, consistent with its interpretation of House Bill 5066. 1 ERCOT included

the completed 765-kV transmission lines as part of its “default” base case in the 2024 and 2025

Regional Transmission Plans but did not independently reevaluate the need for them. 2

        5.       Applicants submitted this project as a reliability project that will benefit the

Permian Basin region. 3 This project is not justified on economic criteria. 4 While the Joint

Applicants propose that there will be other fringe benefits, the standard expressly requires that the

project’s need, specifically reliability and the establishment of additional load-serving capacity, be

established by an ERCOT study for the near future. 5

        6.       Additionally, this project is centered on import to the Permian Basin, not export.

As the PBRP found, “conventional generations are concentrated in the East, Coast, and central

Texas near the load centers” and “due to the significant amounts of loads and lack of local

conventional generation in the Permian Basin region, significant amounts of the regional

transmission upgrades will be needed to transfer power to the Permian Basin region from across

    B. Two Lines Are Sufficient for Non-Large-Load Demand Through 2038.

        7.       Each line of this project has a rated capacity of 7,131 MVA. 8 Using the power factor

of 0.97 applied in the PBRP study, each line delivers 6,917 MW. 9 In 2024, the total Permian Basin

demand was 8,491 MW. The PBRP’s estimate for oil and gas load in 2038 is 14,705 MW. The

incremental difference of 6,214 MW is well within the capacity of a single line.

        8.       The PBRP’s outage assumption is “loss of single generating unit, transmission

circuit, transformer, or common tower outage.” 10 Under the N-1 standard, as long as each line

individually covers the incremental non-large-load demand, one line can be out without requiring

the non-765-kV system to carry the increment. Therefore, two lines comfortably cover oil and gas

and non-large load demands in the region through 2038.

        9.       More precisely, the incremental oil and gas plus all other non-large-load need in

the PBRP is 2,193 MW in 2030 and 4,934 MW in 2038. 11 A single 765-kV transmission line can

support the raw non-large-load forecasted numbers independently. Therefore, the question is how

much weight to assign large-load forecasts, and whether ratepayers should be burdened to fund

import capacity for speculative loads that may locate elsewhere or not at all. 12

      C. Large-Load Forecasts Are Too Speculative to Justify A Third Line.

        10.     The Legislature directed the PUC to consider large load transmission, but it is not

Texas public policy to serve all speculative loads at any cost. The Commission maintains discretion

to balance the interests of ratepayers, public input, and community impact. The Commission

appropriately exercised this discretion when it gave ERCOT good cause to consider only 27.6%

of estimated large-load demand in the 2025 RTP. 13 Similar policy caution is reflected in Governor

Abbot’s June 10th letter to PUC Chairman Thomas Gleeson and ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas. 14 In

regard to data center infrastructure costs, Governor Abbott directed PUC and ERCOT to prevent

costs from being passed to residential ratepayers, safeguard small business ratepayers, and

consider the impact on community water needs. 15

        11.     The “North to Far West” and “South to Far West” Generic Transmission

Constraints (GTC’s) that Applicants cite have never been triggered. Those GTC’s were created in

September 2025. 16 Even assuming 2024 demand as the starting point – demand that was met

without any GTC – and assuming all incremental demand must be served by import, two lines are

sufficient for non-large-load growth through 2038.

     D. Import Path 2 Should Be the Lowest Priority.

        12.     This project, proposing to transmit power out of Bell County East, should be the

lowest priority of the proposed Permian Basin import paths. The 2025 Real Time Transport

Protocol (RTP) states that “Central Texas faces the challenge of needing additional import

capability. To meet the higher projected load demand in Central Texas, new flow patterns have

emerged with imports to Central Texas coming from north of Austin and the Coast Weather Zone.

          15.     ERCOT’s sequencing study prioritized the north and south lines for the 2030 in-

STEP lines in its 2030 and 2031 starting base cases, but that is merely a base-case assumption, not

          16.     Therefore, if the Commission makes the prudent decision to proceed with two

import paths and delay the third, Import Paths 1 and 3 should move forward and Import Path 2

should be delayed. Put another way, this CCN Amendment should be denied.

III.      ROUTE 392’S HABITABLE STRUCTURE COUNT DOES NOT PRECLUDE ITS

          RECOMMENDATION WHEN WEIGHED AGAINST THE FULL SET OF

       A. All 122 Filed Routes Comply with the Policy of Prudent Avoidance, and Route 392’s
          Habitable Structure Count Falls Within the Acceptable Range of Performance Across
          the Routes.

          17.     Many intervenors opposing Route 392, including Hodge & Schwertner, U3

Landowners, and others, center their opposition on Route 392’s habitable structure count.

          18.     The Applicants confirmed at the Hearing on the Merits that all 1,246 EA route links,

and all 122 routes filed with the CCN Application, abide by the policy of prudent avoidance. 28

That should inform how the ALJs weigh Route 392’s habitable structure count. In response to a

of the filed routes, conflicts with the Applicants’ own acknowledgment that every filed route

      B. The Habitable Structure Count is a Regulatory Proxy for Prudent Avoidance, Not a
        Mathematical Determinant of Route Selection.

        20.     Prudent avoidance as defined in the Commission’s Substantive Rule is a policy of

limiting EMF exposure to humans through reasonable investment. The habitable structure count

is a regulatory proxy (it measures structures, not people) and it is not the same thing as prudent

avoidance itself. Former PUC Chairman Smitherman confirmed on cross-examination 33 that the

habitable structure count is a proxy and that route selection on this criterion alone reduces a policy

judgment to a simple math problem, a proposition he rejected. PUC witness Poole further

confirmed that the Commission’s definition of prudent avoidance does not mention habitable

structures, and that the 500-foot notice distance in the rules applies to who receives notice, not to

prudent avoidance itself. Elevating the habitable structure count above hard infrastructure

paralleling, which the legislature expressly identified as a policy preference, risks a misapplication

of the statutory criteria designed to serve route selection.

        21.     The habitable structure counts as applied in this proceeding measure the number of

structures within 500 feet of an alternative route’s centerline. It is count of physical structures, not

of the people within them, and not of how close any given structure is to the transmission line

within that 500-foot band. Former Chairman Smitherman testified that habitable structure counts

are sometimes considered a “proxy” for an imperfect attempt to measure prudent avoidance. But

even if the objective of “prudent avoidance” is to limit electromagnetic exposure to humans,

Smitherman testified that selecting routes on the basis of habitable structure counts alone

improperly reduces a nuanced policy judgment to a simple math exercise. 34 And the Applicants’

own witness Brenda Perkins confirmed that the 500-foot notice distance identifies who receives

notice, not the threshold of prudent avoidance compliance. 35 When Smitherman was asked a

 hypothetical about whether a route with fewer structures would necessarily better satisfy prudent

avoidance if all other factors were held equal, he rejected that proposition: “I think you are trying

to make this a math question. It’s not a math question. It’s a balancing of factors.” 36

        22.      Habitable structure counts as a proxy for prudent avoidance comes with inherent

limitations that were made clear throughout this proceeding. For example, two routes may each

have 100 habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, with all 100 structures on one route

concentrated within 250 feet of the line and all 100 structures on the other route located between

450 and 500 feet away. The counts are identical, but the actual EMF exposure is materially

different. The Commission’s rules do not require a sub-500-foot analysis, and the Applicants did

not conduct one.

        23.      Dr. Mark Turnbough testified on behalf of the Brady Creek Intervenors that the

difference in habitable structures between Route 894 and Route 392 (85 versus 136) is numerically

insignificant when considered in light of the respective route lengths of 223.17 miles and 229.02

miles. 37 No other witness with routing expertise offered a contrary methodology, and none

produced a published standard by which any particular per-mile habitable structure differential

could be characterized as significant or insignificant as a matter of general application. 38 The

Applicants offered no rebuttal to Dr. Turnbough’s analysis of the habitable structure count on

cross-examination and none in their rebuttal testimony.

        24.      Route 392’s habitable-structure count does not preclude the Commission from

recommending it, and the record provides no principled basis for treating the habitable structure

           25.     Certain additional Intervenor arguments will be addressed below. However, Solana

IV.        REPLY TO E6 INTERVENORS.

           26.     E6 Intervenors criticize Solana’s position as exclusively focusing on Solana’s

development plans to the detriment of others.

           27.     This criticism ignores the work Solana has done and will continue to do to foster

wildlife habitat in the area, including as part of its planned development.

           28.     Further, Route 392 does not utilize Segment E6.

           29.     Solana Ranch is not a speculative development, but an active, legally constituted

project backed by substantial governmental and financial commitments. The Texas Legislature

formally created Solana Ranch Municipal Utility District No. 1 through House Bill 5367, effective

June 2023, authorizing up to one billion dollars in bond issuance. 39 Both Williamson and Bell

Counties have executed development agreements, long-term water and wastewater service

arrangements are in place, approximately $10 million in pre-development investment has been

committed, and site work has commenced. 40 Despite the project’s advanced status, the Applicants’

routing witness acknowledged on cross-examination that the routing analysis underlying Route

did not examine preliminary plats or civil engineering contracts in the study area. 41 Route 894 was

therefore selected without any meaningful accounting for Solana Ranch’s actual development

          30.       Route 392 is also the superior alternative route when weighed against all statutory

factors. Dr. Andrew Sansom, former Executive Director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife

Department, testified about the conservation significance of the Colorado River crossing and the

superiority of Link U3. 42 Don Al Ringler testified about the impact of Route 894 on Ringler Ranch,

a separate 270-acre property managed for wildlife habitat and conservation. 43 The Solana

Intervenors’ position is not that the Commission should protect one developer’s investment; it is

that Route 894 fails the applicable legal criteria for every affected landowner, every sensitive

environmental resource, and every community value that PURA § 37.056 (c)(4) was enacted to

protect.

V.        REPLY TO HODGE AND SCHWERTNER.

          31.       Throughout this proceeding, Hodge & Schwertner have artfully attempted to

portray Links E12 and E6 as one unit on habitable structure count. The ALJs should see that effort

for what it is: a red herring designed to prevent consideration of Route 392 on its merits.

          32.       First, habitable structure counts are evaluated on a route basis, not on a link basis.

          33.       Second, Route 392 does not utilize Link E6, which has 77 habitable structures. It is

Link E6 that PUC Staff witness Poole testified was his only “no go” link in the Study Area. Hodge

& Schwertner attempt to ride along on the coattails of that position, even though Poole was clear

as to its limits.

            34.      Link E12 is certainly opposed by Hodge & Schwertner and does have 40 habitable

structures of Route 392’s 136. Again, habitable structures are evaluated on a route-wide basis.

However, the continued emphasis on Link E12 cuts both ways. The rest of Route 392, other than

Link E12, performs quite well on a habitable structure basis. The Commission evaluates habitable

structure counts on a route-wide basis for a reason. All the routes satisfy the Commission policy

of prudent avoidance. Hodge & Schwertner’s “must avoid E12” argument would have the tail

wagging the dog.

           35.      Schwertner further criticizes Solana’s position as focusing on a speculative planned

development. That criticism blithely ignores that Schwertner’s own testimony focused on

opposition to certain links that would inhibit Schwertner’s planned future development, and that

Route 392 does not cross land owned by Schwertner. 44

VI.        CONCLUSION AND PRAYER.

           36.      As set out in Section II of this Reply Brief, the Solana Intervenors urge the ALJs

and the Commission to find that the Applicants have not met their burden of demonstrating the

need for Import Path 2. Simply put, the demand projections the Applicants cite may justify two

Import Paths to the Permian Basin, but do not justify three. Import Path 2 is by far the most

constrained of the three proposed Import Paths. Therefore, this CCN Amendment application

should be denied. Import Paths 1 and 3 will satisfy the needs established by the HB 5066 process.

           37.      In the event the Commission elects to move forward with Import Path 2, Route 392

should be selected. There is no easy choice in this highly constrained study area. However, as set

out in the Initial Brief of the Solana Intervenors and in this Reply Brief, Route 392 best balances

environmental impact, human impact, and financial performance.

    B. Two Lines Are Sufficient for Non-Large-Load Demand Through 2038.

         7.       Each line ofthis project has a rated cap acity of 7,1 3 1 MVA . 8 Using the power factor

of 0.97 applied in the PBRP study, each line delivers 6,917 MW.' In 2024, the total Permian Basin

demand was 8,491 MW. The PBRP's estimate for oil and gas load in 2038 is 14,705 MW. The

incremental difference of 6,214 MW is well within the capacity of a single line.

         8.       The PBRP's outage assumption is "loss of single generating unit, transmission

circuit, transformer, or common tower outage."10 Under the N-1 standard, as long as each line

individually covers the incremental non-large-load demand, one line can be out without requiring

the non-765-kV system to carry the increment. Therefore, two lines comfortably cover oil and gas

and non-large load demands in the region through 2038.

         9.       More precisely, the incremental oil and gas plus all other non-large-load need in

the PBRP is 2,193 MW in 2030 and 4,934 MW in 2038.11 A single 765-kV transmission line can

support the raw non-large-load forecasted numbers independently. Therefore, the question is how

much weight to assign large-load forecasts, and whether ratepayers should be burdened to fund

import capacity for speculative loads that may locate elsewhere or not at all. 12

     C. Large-Load Forecasts Are Too Speculative to Justify A Third Line.

        10.     The Legislature directed the PUC to consider large load transmission, but it is not

Texas public policy to serve all speculative loads at any cost. The Commission maintains discretion

to balance the interests of ratepayers, public input, and community impact. The Commission

appropriately exercised this discretion when it gave ERCOT good cause to consider only 27.6%

of estimated large-load demand in the 2025 RTP.13 Similar policy caution is reflected in Governor

Abbot's June 101h letter to PUC Chairman Thomas Gleeson and ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas. 14 In

regard to data center infrastructure costs, Governor Abbott directed PUC and ERCOT to prevent

costs from being passed to residential ratepayers, safeguard small business ratepayers, and

consider the impact on community water needs. 15

        11.     The "North to Far West" and "South to Far West" Generic Transmission

Constraints (GTC's) that Applicants cite have never been triggered. Those GTC' s were created in

September 2025.16 Even assuming 2024 demand as the starting point - demand that was met

without any GTC - and assuming all incremental demand must be served by import, two lines are

sufficient for non-large-load growth through 2038.

     B. The Habitable Structure Count is a Regulatory Proxy for Prudent Avoidance, Not a
       Mathematical Determinant of Route Selection.

        20.     Prudent avoidance as defined in the Commission's Substantive Rule is a policy of

limiting EMF exposure to humans through reasonable investment. The habitable structure count

is a regulatory proxy (it measures structures, not people) and it is not the same thing as prudent

avoidance itself. Former PUC Chairman Smitherman confirmed on cross-examination33 that the

habitable structure count is a proxy and that route selection on this criterion alone reduces a policy

judgment to a simple math problem, a proposition he rejected. PUC witness Poole further

confirmed that the Commission' s definition of prudent avoidance does not mention habitable

structures, and that the 500-foot notice distance in the rules applies to who receives notice, not to

prudent avoidance itself. Elevating the habitable structure count above hard infrastructure

paralleling, which the legislature expressly identified as a policy preference, risks a misapplication

of the statutory criteria designed to serve route selection.

        21.     The habitable structure counts as applied in this proceeding measure the number of

structures within 500 feet of an alternative route' s centerline. It is count of physical structures, not

of the people within them, and not of how close any given structure is to the transmission line

within that 500-foot band. Former Chairman Smitherman testified that habitable structure counts

are sometimes considered a "proxy" for an imperfect attempt to measure prudent avoidance. But

even if the objective of "prudent avoidance" is to limit electromagnetic exposure to humans,

Smitherman testified that selecting routes on the basis of habitable structure counts alone

improperly reduces a nuanced policy judgment to a simple math exercise.34 And the Applicants'

own witness Brenda Perkins confirmed that the 500-foot notice distance identifies who receives

notice, not the threshold of prudent avoidance compliance.35 When Smitherman was asked a

VI.      CONCLUSION AND PRAYER.

         36.      As set out in Section II of this Reply Brief, the Solana Intervenors urge the ALJs

and the Commission to find that the Applicants have not met their burden of demonstrating the

need for Import Path 2. Simply put, the demand projections the Applicants cite may justify two

Import Paths to the Permian Basin, but do not justify three. Import Path 2 is by far the most

constrained of the three proposed Import Paths. Therefore, this CCN Amendment application

should be denied. Import Paths 1 and 3 will satisfy the needs established by the HB 5066 process.

         37.      In the event the Commission elects to move forward with Import Path 2, Route 392

should be selected. There is no easy choice in this highly constrained study area. However, as set

environmental impact, human impact, and financial performance.
